According to the latest report by Counterpoint Research, pricing pressure from rising memory costs has squeezed the U.S. budget smartphone market in the second quarter of 2026, with smaller manufacturers hit particularly hard, as larger brands are better positioned to absorb rising component costs. Details are as follows.

Rising memory costs hit low-end smartphones the hardest

According to Counterpoint Research data, combined U.S. smartphone sales of Apple, Samsung, Motorola and Google fell 4% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, while sales of the rest of the market plunged 45%, reflecting how smaller manufacturers struggled to stay afloat amid rising component costs.

Counterpoint noted that sales of smartphones priced under US$100 fell by nearly 65% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026. Rising component costs have narrowed the price gap between Samsung's and Motorola's entry-level handsets and white-label phones, enabling these two brands to expand their share of the prepaid market.

As for Apple, the report noted that while Apple has not adjusted iPhone pricing in the United States, it has raised prices on other products. Counterpoint expects Apple "to raise pricing on the iPhone 18 series," with some models expected to be unveiled in the coming weeks.

Highlights from the report:

Analyst Jeff Pu already predicted last week that the iPhone 18 Pro would be priced between US$1,349 and US$1,399, the iPhone 18 Pro Max between US$1,449 and US$1,499, with multiple reports also indicating the iPhone Ultra would start at around US$2,500.

Apple reported its fiscal third-quarter 2026 results late last month, with iPhone revenue rising 22% year-on-year to US$54.2 billion. The company also warned that memory costs and supply constraints would worsen significantly in the September quarter, particularly for iPhone, iPad and Mac.
